idiom_name: CanActivate guard (UseGuards/APP_GUARD) plus an interceptor for audit
implementation_notes: NestJS makes the secure action explicit: a CanActivate guard runs before the handler, reads route metadata through Reflector and returns false or throws to short-circuit, and can be bound per-controller, per-method or globally through APP_GUARD, so one class carries the shared check sequence. Interceptors wrap the handler when the shared step must surround it rather than gate it. Guards and interceptors are the framework's own pipeline, so no base class hierarchy is needed.
pitfalls: Guards run after middleware and before interceptors and pipes, so a check placed in the wrong stage sees the wrong data (unparsed body, missing route metadata).
A global guard registered with useGlobalGuards() cannot inject dependencies; register it through an APP_GUARD provider instead.
Returning false yields the framework's generic ForbiddenException; throw a specific exception when the API promises a stable error shape.

variants.name: Express middleware stack with typed request augmentation
variants.idiom_name: ordered RequestHandler array mounted before the routes
variants.implementation_notes: Outside NestJS the shared sequence is an ordered Express middleware stack applied with app.use, with TypeScript contributing only the request augmentation types (user, session) and the middleware signatures. The base-handler idea survives as a security router or an array of RequestHandler mounted before the routes; the classic class structure adds nothing in this style.
pitfalls: Handlers registered before the security stack are unguarded; mount the stack at the router root and test for coverage.
The augmented Request type is a compile-time claim only; runtime code must not assume req.user exists when a route skipped the stack.
